Triggers.value: Specific body parts associated with the event
Night-time or waking up in the dark

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Going to sleep or lying in the dark

Memory.value: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear
The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over

issues.item: Escape Route Planning: always plan an escape route before entering a place
issues.explanation: 'Always plan an escape route before entering a place' implies a persistent current external-danger / entrapment threat style that is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which centers on intrusive sensory memory linked to the child's illness (body parts, darkness, songs; reliving, fragments, present-tense memory). For trauma of a child's life-threatening illness, this strategy is clinically much less coherent than avoidance/sleep delay, and it is not supported by any Threat or Appraisal items. Given the formulation, Triggers and Memory are strongly linked, but this item reflects a different syndrome focus (situational escape/safety behavior) not represented elsewhere in the selected nodes.

vignette:
Kiet is a 42-year-old Hmong farmer who lives with his wife and their surviving son on a small plot in California’s Central Valley. Eighteen months ago, his younger son, Bao, then five, was diagnosed with acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Bao spent four months in the pediatric oncology unit, and Kiet was with him every night—sleeping on a vinyl chair, listening to the beeping monitors, watching the IV line snake into Bao’s small arm. The moment that lodged itself deepest was the night of the first sepsis crisis: Bao’s skin went grey, his eyes rolled back, and for two hours Kiet held him while the doctors worked. Bao survived, but Kiet did not.

In the months after the discharge, Kiet began to notice that certain things would send him straight back to that hospital room. At first it was the sight of a child’s thin arm with a bandage or a bruise—he would freeze, his heart hammering, the smell of antiseptic flooding his nose. Then he realized that any darkness, especially waking up at two in the morning to an unlit bedroom, would bring the memory surging back with such force that he could feel Bao’s weight against his chest again. And there was a song—a lullaby his wife used to hum, *Sleep, My Baby*—that played once on the radio in his truck and left him shaking in the parking lot of the feed store, the tears so sudden he had to pull over. He learned to avoid the radio altogether.

The memories themselves were not like normal remembering. They came as fragments—the silver gleam of a suture needle, the pale curve of Bao’s knee—and they did not feel past. When a memory arrived, Kiet was no longer in the present; he was back in that chair, the terror fresh. The fragments emerged without warning, triggered by a shadow, a sound, a stray patch of darkness outside the window. And the more the memories came, the more Kiet’s brain seemed to scan for the things that could set them off. He started noticing the dark more often—checking the corners of the barn as the sun went down, his stomach tightening before he even knew why.

Kiet’s strategies for coping grew slowly, like a habit he did not choose. He began avoiding people: his wife’s questions, the neighbour who wanted to talk about his own son’s soccer game, the farmhand who hummed something tunelessly—all of it felt unbearable. He would work alone in the farthest field, or find an excuse to leave if company came. But the hardest part was sleep. Going to bed meant lying in the dark, and the dark meant the memory. So Kiet started staying up until one or two in the morning, watching late-night TV with the volume low, or walking the farmyard until his legs ached. He avoided lying down altogether until he was so exhausted that he would collapse on the couch. But even then, the dark would find him. The avoidance looped back on itself: because he stayed awake, he was more likely to be in the dark at odd hours, his senses sharpened, waiting for a fragment to hit. And because the memories were so vivid, he was more determined the next night not to go to bed. His wife slept alone now, and he could feel the distance growing between them.

What brought Kiet to a therapist was not the avoidance itself but a morning when his older son asked him why he never looked at Bao anymore. Kiet realized he had been avoiding his surviving son’s body, too—the curve of a shoulder, a new freckle—because every part of a child seemed to carry the echo of that hospital arm. He was exhausted, hollowed out, and frightened by what his mind was doing. He was hoping, without quite believing it, that talking could somehow unhook the dark from the memory, that there was a way to sleep again without waking up in a room that was not the present.
